content: Chlorhexidine is a broad-spectrum topical antiseptic that is effective against both aerobic and anaerobic microorganisms. It has been shown to reduce bacterial colonization in neonates and may help prevent infections. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of chlorhexidine for neonatal skin or umbilical cord care compared to routine care or no treatment in reducing infections and mortality in late preterm or term newborns in both hospital and community settings. The review included 12 trials, with seven conducted in hospitals and five in community settings. In some studies, maternal vaginal cleansing with chlorhexidine was also performed in addition to neonatal skin and cord care. Findings in Hospital Settings: 1. Chlorhexidine Cord Cleansing vs. Dry Cord Care: Low-quality evidence from one trial suggested no significant difference in neonatal mortality (RR 0.11, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.04). Moderate-quality evidence from two trials indicated that chlorhexidine cord cleansing likely reduces the risk of omphalitis or infections (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.84). 2. Chlorhexidine Skin Cleansing vs. Dry Cord Care: Low-quality evidence from two trials suggested no significant difference in the risk of omphalitis or infections (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.39). None of the studies in this comparison reported effects on neonatal mortality. Findings in Community Settings: 1. Chlorhexidine Cord Cleansing vs. Dry Cord Care: High-quality evidence from three trials demonstrated that chlorhexidine cord cleansing reduces neonatal mortality (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.71 to 0.92) and the risk of omphalitis or infections (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.57). 2. Chlorhexidine Skin Cleansing vs. Usual Skin Care: High-quality evidence from one trial showed no significant difference in neonatal mortality (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.23). None of the studies in this comparison reported effects on omphalitis or infections. Maternal Vaginal Chlorhexidine in Addition to Neonatal Cleansing: 1. In Hospital Settings: Moderate-quality evidence from one trial showed no significant difference in neonatal mortality when maternal vaginal chlorhexidine was used in addition to total body cleansing (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.42). High-quality evidence from two trials showed no significant difference in the risk of infections (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.16). One trial reported an increased risk of hypothermia with maternal vaginal cleansing and total body cleansing (RR 1.33, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.49). 2. In Community Settings: Low-quality evidence from one trial suggested no significant difference in neonatal mortality (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.03). Moderate-quality evidence from one trial indicated that maternal vaginal chlorhexidine in addition to total body cleansing likely reduces the risk of neonatal infections (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.95). These studies did not report effects on omphalitis. Authors' Conclusions: The effect of chlorhexidine applied to umbilical cords in hospital settings on neonatal mortality remains uncertain due to low-quality evidence. Chlorhexidine cord care in community settings is supported by high-quality evidence, showing a 50% reduction in omphalitis and a 12% reduction in neonatal mortality. Maternal vaginal chlorhexidine in hospital settings likely does not affect neonatal mortality or infection risk. In community settings, the effect of maternal vaginal chlorhexidine on mortality outcomes is uncertain due to small sample sizes and low event rates.
